Required mechanisms:
(C) Characterization: an integer m >= a_1 is a term iff its prime support meets the prime support of every term (equivalently every earlier term). Section 1 proves this: (1) states m is a term iff P(m) is good, where good means E ∩ P(a_i) ≠ ∅ for every i ≥ 1. The proof: forward by pairwise non-coprimality; converse: if m not a term, pick n with a_n < m < a_{n+1} (using unboundedness), then m cannot share prime factor with all of a_1..a_n else a_{n+1} ≤ m; hence m coprime to some term. Wait — need to handle m ≤ a_1? They say "for every integer m ≥ A". If m ≥ A and m is not a term... if m < a_2 and m ≠ A then a_1 < m < a_2 works with n=1. If m = A it's a term. If m > A but m < a_1? Not possible since m ≥ A = a_1. Hmm, what if m ≥ A, m not a term, then m > a_1 (since a_1 = A ≤ m and m ≠ A). So there's n with a_n < m < a_{n+1} by unboundedness. Fine. This is a correct proof of (C). Score 2.

(F) Finiteness / large-prime erasure: membership depends only on primes in a finite set (e.g., primes ≤ a_1 or ≤ a_1^2), because any term divisible by a large prime is dominated by a smaller number with same small-prime support that is itself a term — proved for ALL terms.

Section 2: Lemma: for every sequence term x, σ(x) = P(x) ∩ Q (Q = primes ≤ A) is good. Proof by induction over terms in increasing order. Given x with a prime factor q > A. R = product of primes in σ(x), pick p ∈ σ(x), k ≥ 0 least with m = R p^k ≥ A. Then P(m) = σ(x), m < x (two cases shown). Wait — need σ(x) nonempty, which they establish first (every term shares a prime with A, which is ≤ A; well, the common prime divisor of x and A is at most A indeed since it divides A). Good.

Check m < x: If k = 0: m = R < Rq ≤ x since q | x and q ∤ R (q > A, R product of primes ≤ A). Actually need R | x/q... R divides x (all primes of σ(x) divide x, to first power at least; R is squarefree product). x ≥ R·q since R | x, q | x, q ∤ R, and x > 1... Actually x could equal Rq? They claim m < x i.e. R < Rq ≤ x. If x = R·q exactly, then R < x. OK.

If k > 0: R p^{k-1} < A, so p^k < pA/R ≤ A (since p ≤ A, p/R ≤ ... wait p ≤ A and R ≥ p, so p/R ≤ 1, p·A/R ≤ A). Hmm, they wrote p^k < pA/R ≤ A < q. So m = R p^k < R q ≤ x. Good.

Then: if m = A it's a term; else m > A. Suppose m not a term; then by the proof of (1), there's a term b < m with gcd(b, m) = 1. Since b < m < x, induction hypothesis: σ(b) good, so σ(b) meets P(x) (since P(x) ⊇ σ(x), and goodness of σ(b) means it meets every P(a_i), and x is a term... wait, induction: b is a term smaller than x, so σ(b) good means σ(b) meets P of every term, including P(x)). Meanwhile σ(b) ∩ σ(x) = ∅ (since σ(b) ⊆ P(b), gcd(b,m)=1, σ(x) = P(m); so every prime dividing b is coprime to m hence not in P(m) = σ(x)). All primes of σ(b) ≤ A; all primes of P(x) \ σ(x) > A. So σ(b) ∩ P(x) = ∅, contradicting goodness. Hence m is a term, so P(m) = σ(x) good. Induction complete.

Wait — there's a subtle issue: the induction is over sequence terms in increasing order, i.e., a_1, a_2, ...; "Since b < x, the induction hypothesis says σ(b) is good" — b is a sequence term less than x, so by strong induction σ(b) good. Also need x itself to be a term when applying σ(b) meets P(x): σ(b) good means it meets P(a_i) for every i ≥ 1 — but wait, that includes terms larger than x too. Goodness defined as meeting all terms' supports. Hmm, but the induction hypothesis only gives σ(b) good per the lemma statement which is "σ(b) is good", i.e., meets P(a_i) for all i. Actually the induction hypothesis is the lemma for all earlier terms: σ(b) good. Goodness means σ(b) ∩ P(a_i) ≠ ∅ for every i ≥ 1, in particular for x = a_j: σ(b) ∩ P(x) ≠ ∅. Fine — actually the lemma statement "σ(x) is good" quantifies over all i, including future terms relative to x. Hmm, but then to prove it by induction we'd need... The lemma for x is: σ(x) meets P(a_i) for all i. The proof shows: if all prime factors of x ≤ A, σ(x) = P(x) good by (1). Otherwise construct m with P(m) = σ(x) and show m is a term; then σ(x) = P(m) is good by (1). This doesn't actually need induction for the conclusion about x itself! Wait: in the contradiction argument, to show m is a term they used induction hypothesis on b < m < x. So induction is used to establish that m is a term (i.e., to rule out existence of the coprime smaller term). Hmm, actually they use: suppose m not a term, then exists term b < m with gcd(b,m) = 1. Actually wait, do they even need induction? If m not a term, there's b < m with gcd(b,m)=1, b a term. Then σ(b) ⊆ P(b), and gcd(b, m) = 1 so P(b) ∩ P(m) = ∅, so σ(b) ∩ σ(x) = ∅. So no contradiction directly; induction is needed. Indeed the induction hypothesis is essential: σ(b) good means σ(b) meets P(x); contradiction. Right, that's why induction. And the induction is valid: b < m < x, b a term preceding x in the sequence, so the strong induction hypothesis applies. Good.

Hmm wait, one more check: in the case m = A, "then it is already the first sequence term". m = R p^k ≥ A with m = A. Fine.

Also the claim "P(m) = σ(x)": m = R p^k where R = product of distinct primes in σ(x) and p ∈ σ(x), so P(m) = σ(x). Yes.

Then (3): m is a term iff P(m) good iff σ(m) good. Forward: P(m) good (by (1)) and lemma gives σ(m) good? Wait lemma gives σ(m) good for terms m. Forward direction of second equivalence: m term ⇒ σ(m) good — that's the lemma. Reverse: σ(m) good ⇒ P(m) ⊇ σ(m) good ⇒ m term by (1). Good.

So (F) is fully proved: membership depends only on primes ≤ A. Score 2. This is the large-prime erasure done for all terms via the R p^k construction — a complete argument. Note the mechanism differs slightly from the sketch in the grading instructions ("dominated by a smaller number with the same small-prime support that is itself a term") — indeed that's exactly what's done: m = R p^k < x, P(m) = σ(x), m is a term. (P) Periodicity assembly: Section 3. L = product of primes ≤ A. For m ≥ A, p | m+L iff p | m for p ∈ Q, so σ(m+L) = σ(m), so by (3), m term iff m+L term for all m ≥ A. Global from the first term. T = number of terms in [A, A+L-1]. Each block of L consecutive integers in [A, ∞) contains exactly T terms. Then (a_n, a_n + L] contains exactly T terms and right endpoint is a term, so a_{n+T} = a_n + L. 

Wait, check: the interval (a_n, a_n + L] contains exactly T terms — it's L consecutive integers, contained in [A, ∞) since a_n ≥ A. The terms in it, including the right endpoint a_n + L which is a term (since a_n is a term and a_n ≥ A... wait, need (4) applied: a_n term and a_n ≥ A ⇒ a_n + L term. Yes.) Hmm, "contains exactly T terms" — each window of length L has exactly T terms by periodicity (residue classes mod L). The number of terms in (a_n, a_n+L] equals number in [a_n+1, a_n+L], which is T. The terms strictly after a_n are a_{n+1}, a_{n+2}, ...; exactly T of them are ≤ a_n + L, and a_n + L is a term, hence a_{n+T} = a_n + L. Correct.

Actually wait, one subtlety: a_{n+T} ≤ a_n + L < a_{n+T+1}. Since exactly T terms lie in (a_n, a_n+L], the T-th one after a_n is ≤ a_n + L and is the largest ≤ a_n+L; since a_n+L is itself a term, the T-th one equals a_n + L. Yes.

Answer (structure): L = product of all primes ≤ a_1, T = number of terms in a window of length L. Explicitly stated. Score 2.

Wrong answer stated? No — they prove global periodicity from n=1, and they even note the distinction from eventual periodicity in falsification item 3. The false lemma about minimal hitting sets is not used; they explicitly falsify related naive hypotheses. The proof seems complete and correct.
